opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that they're useful, but they're not sufficient on their own, and we have to be careful not to overestimate what they bring to the physical world.

Language models are very good at abstraction. They've compressed an enormous amount of human knowledge, so they understand concepts, they can plan at a high level, they can tell you that a cup should go on a table rather than under it. That's genuinely valuable as a kind of common-sense prior. But language is a lossy description of the world. When you say "pick up the cup," the words don't contain the friction, the weight distribution, the exact geometry of the handle, how the liquid sloshes. All of that physical detail is precisely what a robot or any embodied system needs to act correctly, and it's mostly absent from text.

Vision models get closer, because images and videos are direct observations of the physical world. But most of them were trained to recognize, to classify, or to generate things that look plausible to a human viewer. Looking plausible and being physically correct are two different objectives. A generated video can look beautiful while objects pass through each other or violate basic dynamics. And recognition models tell you "this is a chair," but they don't necessarily tell you where you can push it, how it will move, or what happens in three dimensions when you interact with it.

So when I assess them, I usually ask a few questions. First, does the model represent the world in 3D and over time, or is it still fundamentally 2D and static? Second, does it capture cause and effect? If I take an action, can it predict the consequence? Third, can it be grounded in actual sensor data and action spaces, not just pixels and tokens? Most existing models score reasonably on the first, partially, and poorly on the second and third.

That's why I think of current language and vision models as strong foundations or components rather than the final answer. They give you semantics and perception. What's missing is something like a world model: a representation that understands geometry, physics, and interaction, and can simulate what will happen. Building that layer, and figuring out how to connect it with the knowledge already inside language and vision models, is where I think the real work for physical-world AI is right now.

r001.rationale: The candidate says language omits physical details needed for action; it does not express that digital and physical worlds do not differ substantially at the language level.

r002.rationale: The candidate says vision models are often developed for recognition, classification, or human-plausible generation, while physical applications require physical correctness and interaction understanding.

fable-5.1.text:
I think we should be honest about what these models actually are. Language models and even today's vision-language models were trained almost entirely on internet data, meaning text, images, and video that humans produced and uploaded. That data is a record of how humans describe and depict the world. It is not a record of how the world itself behaves. So when we ask whether these models understand physics, I would say they have learned a kind of commonsense summary of the physical world, the way a person who has only read books and watched videos might, but they have never actually touched anything.

That matters a lot once you move to the physical world. In language, if a model is 90 percent right, that is very useful, because a human reads the output and corrects the rest. In a robot, 90 percent means the cup is dropped one time in ten, and nobody will accept that. Physical tasks demand a level of precision and consistency that the internet-trained models were simply never optimized for. They are strong on semantics, on knowing what an object is and roughly what you do with it, but weak on geometry, contact, force, and the fine details of time and causality.

A second gap is the data itself. There is essentially no large corpus of "interaction data" on the internet, data where an agent acts and the world responds. Every piece of robot data today is collected by hand, by teleoperation, in small quantities, on specific hardware. So we are missing the equivalent of the trillions of tokens that made language models work. That is why I think the field is converging on world models and simulation: if you cannot collect enough real interaction data, you try to learn a model of the world that can generate it, and you use the vision and language models as the prior, the source of semantics and commonsense, rather than as the controller itself.

So my assessment is: existing models are an excellent starting point and a poor finishing point. Treat them as the brain's knowledge layer, then build the perception, physical prediction, and control layers that they fundamentally lack. Anyone who expects to simply fine-tune a vision-language model and get a reliable robot is going to be disappointed.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes that internet data records human depictions rather than how the physical world behaves, and describes substantial gaps in physical understanding. It does not say the digital and physical worlds are similar at the language level.

r002.rationale: The response says these models were trained on internet data and were never optimized for the precision and consistency physical tasks require, so their strengths do not meet physical-world needs.

astra-6.text:
I think existing language and vision models provide a very useful foundation, but there’s still a gap between understanding information and acting in the physical world. A model can describe a scene or explain how to perform a task, yet that doesn’t necessarily mean it can predict what will happen when it takes an action.

In the physical world, you have to understand space, motion, and cause and effect. You also have to deal with incomplete observations and respond to feedback. If you’re picking up a cup, recognizing the cup is only part of the problem. You need to know how to grasp it, how much force to apply, and how to adjust if it slips.

So I would see these models as components of a larger system. Their semantic understanding and general knowledge are valuable, but they need to be connected to perception, action, and learning from interaction. The real test is whether that system can behave reliably when the environment differs from what it has seen before.

r001.rationale: The response describes a gap between understanding information and acting physically, but does not say the digital and physical worlds are similar at the language level.

r002.rationale: The response says models need perception, action, and interaction-based learning, but does not state that the motivations behind digital-world vision models align poorly with physical-world needs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think existing language and vision models provide a useful foundation, but there’s still a gap between understanding information and acting reliably in the physical world. A model may recognize an object or describe a scene very well, yet that doesn’t necessarily mean it understands what will happen when you push that object, grasp it, or move around it.

For physical applications, you need spatial understanding, an understanding of dynamics, and the ability to learn from the consequences of actions. You also need to handle uncertainty: observations are incomplete, environments change, and mistakes have real consequences.

So I would assess these models as valuable components, especially for perception and high-level reasoning. But their suitability has to be demonstrated through interaction and testing in the intended environment. Strong performance on language or image benchmarks alone doesn’t establish that a system can operate reliably in the physical world.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes recognizing or describing information from acting reliably in the physical world; it does not say the digital and physical worlds are similar at the language level.
